scenarios.title: Where does the rain go?
scenarios.subject: Watershed science and local infrastructure
scenarios.question: How might paving change where rainwater goes?
scenarios.knowledge: Some rain infiltrates soil, some evaporates, and some runs over the surface. Surface cover, slope, soil, rainfall intensity and drainage alter the outcome.
prediction: More paved surface often means more runoff
Less paved surface always means more runoff
A model proves the local flood outcome
scenarios.challenge: A grassy surface can also shed runoff if soil is saturated or rainfall is intense. Never assume one variable alone determines a real flood.
scenarios.activity: Use two equal, safely measured small water samples over contrasting surfaces or compare simple paper diagrams. Record observations as model-only and name a measurement you still need.
scenarios.transfer: Apply the same observation-versus-model distinction to a street drain, rain garden or different land surface.
scenarios.sourceLabel: Existing CoAthene Watershed Explorer lesson donor
scenarios.safety: Do not pour water near electronics. Indoor dry/paper alternative is valid. An adult supervises practical activities with minors.

scenarios.title: When is a mirror not equivalent?
scenarios.subject: Digital literacy and careful analogy
scenarios.question: Does mirroring an interface also reverse who is allowed to use it?
scenarios.knowledge: A reflected icon or screen layout changes its visual appearance. Authentication and permissions are separately governed by software rules and authorizations.
prediction: Mirrored icons grant mirrored access permissions
Mirrored icons do not by themselves grant new permissions
A useful visual analogy must always imply identical physical mechanisms
scenarios.challenge: The *question* of symmetry can be reused across subjects, but a software access rule is not a physical parity operator in particle physics.
scenarios.activity: Draw two mirror-image door symbols. List what changed visibly and what did not change about who has permission to enter. Avoid real accounts and credentials.
scenarios.transfer: Use the same distinction between appearance and authorization when critiquing a copycat website or a changed app layout.
scenarios.sourceLabel: Public source on virtual projections versus identity
scenarios.safety: Use only fictional screen mock-ups. Do not test other people's accounts, devices or security controls.

scenarios.title: What makes a shared space work?
scenarios.subject: Civic design, collaboration and responsible decisions
scenarios.question: How could a community improve a shared public place for more people?
scenarios.knowledge: Different participants may value accessibility, shade, safety, cost, quiet, nature and maintenance differently. A plan needs factual site knowledge, legitimate authority and fair opportunity to disagree.
prediction: The first popular proposal is always fair
A single AI ranking can authorize a public change
A good proposal should name who is affected and allow challenge
scenarios.challenge: A design that seems best for one group may obstruct another. A fictional planning exercise does not confer permission to modify public property.
scenarios.activity: Sketch three original proposals for a fictional park, note benefits and trade-offs, then describe a fair feedback route, including non-digital participation.
scenarios.transfer: Carry the same trade-off and consent checks into a classroom, club or shared digital community.
scenarios.safety: Use fictional places and roles. Do not collect real neighbours' personal data or represent the exercise as a council decision.
